quotes.quote: The gridded AORC precipitation dataset contains one-hour accumulated surface-precipitation (APCP) ending at the 'top' of each hour, in liquid water-equivalent units (kg/m^2 to the nearest .01 kg/m^2)

For the duration of the period of record, NLDAS2 daily precipitation was used as the reference for all areas except as noted. From 1979 to 2001, NLDAS2 24-hour totals ending at 1200 UTC were the daily reference over the CONUS. Stage IV daily precipitation, with interactive, manual quality control and the introduction of radar data, has been used since 2002.

Examination of Stage IV daily precipitation showed that, in some areas, it was consistently biased low during the winter months from 2002 to approximately 2009 as a result of limitations in radar capability for precipitation-type discrimination prior to the implementation of dual-polarimetric technology. [...] improved the accuracy of precipitation estimates substantially, from 2010 to the near-present.

the AORC daily precipitation between 1979 and 2015 was bias corrected with monthly accumulated Livneh data, where available. [...] After 2015, the Stage IV daily product was directly used without a bias correction procedure. After daily AORC input forcing data was bias-corrected for the long-term climatology, the daily time series were then disaggregated using available hourly data

AORC daily precipitation during and after 2010 is based on Stage IV, where available, with a bias correction factor, varying by month, applied. The bias correction is set by the ratio of the 6-year accumulations for the Livneh data to the Stage IV data, during 2010-2015.

For the more recent years, Stage IV hourly data has been used to disaggregate the daily precipitation grids blended from several datasets. [...] GDAS hourly precipitation is used to disaggregate the 24-hour AORC values to 1-hour values in the case that remote-sensing information from radar or satellite is unavailable.

Temporal downscaling from daily to hourly precipitation amounts is based on a multiplicative-correction approach. The multiplicative correction approach disaggregates, temporally, daily rainfall amounts to hourly amounts using factors. These factors are calculated by aggregating hourly grids to 0:00, 1:00, 2:00 ...23:00 time steps and dividing these amounts with the coincident daily grids. The hourly grids were calculated from the mosaic of datasets that were applied: Stage IV, GDAS, Stage II, CFSR, CMORPH, WSI NOWrad, and MDR.
The data creation runs with a 10-day lag to ensure the inclusion of any corrections to the input Stage IV and NLDAS data.

observations: Structure of AORC in the test years: hours are Stage IV hours times one factor per gauge day (hourly correlation 0.9995 within a day, ratio CV 0.038, daily ratio median 1.09, p10-p90 0.87-1.41). The factor is shared across local midnight (log-ratio correlation 0.90) and changes more across 12 UTC (0.78) than across placebo times (0.85). On 2010-01-24 (South Fork Holston) the whole gauge day is scaled by 1.9 before and after midnight (24.4 against 47.4 mm, 5.7 against 10.9 mm). The factor is not a constant per calendar month (months explain 6% of its variance in 2010-2014, 14% in 2005-2009). Of 594 rain basin-days, 12 have a pattern that departs from Stage IV's (r below 0.98, lowest 0.884) and 16 a ratio spread above 0.15: where GDAS-like disaggregation could act it is rare.

The networks respond to rain they are given: adding 5% of the after-midnight AORC rain to the hours before midnight adds 13 warnings, 12% adds 28, 100% gives 478 (78%); removing 12% takes 16 away. A leak large enough to explain the gain would have to be several times the rain after midnight, which every measurement excludes.

The gain is concentrated: the NSE gain over the rain table sits in eight basins (+0.07 to +0.22 each: Hyco Creek, Little River, Murder Creek, Turkey Creek, French Broad, South Toe, SF Holston, Leaf River); NE Cape Fear (-0.009), Catawba (+0.005), Charlie Creek (+0.002) and Myakka (-0.058) do not gain.

Keeping the Daymet column beside AORC adds nothing to the onsets (replaced table 315 hits against 313, sign test p = 0.87 on the 40 discordant onsets) and adds 0.035 of NSE (0.767 against 0.732): the Daymet table carries some information on the volume of rain that AORC to midnight lacks, not on the onsets.

The 48 filled hours of 2006-08-11..12 (Murder Creek) are the only ERA5-filled hours inside the test years; the flow was 0.03-0.11 mm/day against a high-flow level of 2.62, no onset lies near. The 264 partly missing hours are all in training years (1986, 1989).

The verdict words of the project's own criteria are unchanged by the new input: onsets NOT YET for every set including the ridge and forest (51% warned, 50% of warnings false; GO needs 70% and 30%), all high-flow days CAUTION (74% warned, 31% false: 0.8 points of far above GO).

Nothing I reviewed changed while I reviewed it (h5).

The training years (1980-2000) are the NLDAS2-total and non-radar-hour period of AORC and the test years are the Stage IV period (the builder's note 7 says what the network learns from a disaggregation of daily totals was not measured separately). My tests concern the test-year inputs, which are what the 51% is scored on; they cannot tell whether a network trained on radar-era hours would do better.

Download volume of this review, to be plain: 1,070 hourly Stage IV files from the Iowa Mesonet archive (1.2 MB each, about 1.3 GB, at most 6 parallel connections, each file read and dropped, only the basin means kept), above the 'about 1 GB' limit of the brief because I planned with 1.1 MB per file; about 4 MB from the NOAA AORC bucket; the methods PDF (1.3 MB) and the registry page (22 KB). No further Stage IV was fetched.
verdict: E1b holds up under independent recomputation, and the hindsight risk I was asked to test hard does not show up in the test years. Every number I could recompute equals the builder's (313 of 611 onsets = 51.2%, single trainings 48.6, 48.6 and 55.3%; controls 17.7, 37.5 and 18.7%; ERA5 30.0%; ridge 55.2%, forest 48.0%; replaced table 51.6%; median NSE 0.767 against 0.590; over 3,000 derived values; the 12 saved networks bit for bit from tables I built myself; the figure to 0.2 point), no hour after a window's end enters any input (90 perturbation cases), the AORC series equals my own reduction of the raw chunks (0.00 mm; 408 filled and 264 partial hours re-read from the raw files), and the engine files changed by another agent are additive and pass their test. On hindsight: the documentation shows that the channel exists by construction (daily totals on a 12 UTC gauge day spread over the hours by Stage IV's hourly shape, so an hour before midnight can carry a factor set by a day that includes rain after the issue time), but on 78 test-year days (the builder's 50 plus 28 I chose by onsets and night storms, which hold 11.8 mm of Stage IV rain after midnight on average against 1.1 mm in the builder's) the AORC rain before midnight does not depend on the Stage IV rain after it (coefficient -0.030, 95% -0.060 to -0.001; 35 dry-before/wet-after basin-days hold 0.08 mm before midnight), and the saved networks given Stage IV, a real-time product, in place of AORC for the issue day warn of 86 to 95 of the 171 onsets of those days against 92 with AORC (the rain table alone: 15). Best estimate of the part of the 51% that could be hindsight: none; at most about 3 points, measured on 28% of the onsets, not proven for the other 440 (about 10-13 GB of Stage IV would cover them). What needs fixing is wording and records, not numbers: the last clause of outcome_full ('the mis-stamped table itself costs skill') is not supported as worded, and the sentence that documents must quote says nothing about AORC being a retrospective analysis; the other items (the NSE-only reading of 'the LSTM is clearly ahead', leads 2-3, the by-period reading, the 88 GB, the log, the reproduction path, the registry announcement) are in should_fix. The 51% is a good measurement of what well-measured rain up to midnight is worth; it is not an operational warning (verdict NOT YET), and its transfer to a real-time service rests on the 171 onsets I could test with Stage IV, not yet on all 611.
